transcript.prompt: According to Euler’s formula, how can you write e^(jωt) using sine and cosine, where j² = −1?

transcript.text: I think it has something to do with e^(jωt) and rotating in the complex plane?

transcript.explanation: You correctly connect complex exponentials with rotation in the complex plane. The required formula is e^(jωt) = cos(ωt) + j sin(ωt), where cosine is the real part and sine is the imaginary part.

transcript.text: You recalled the rotation connection; the missing piece is Euler’s formula: e^(jωt) = cos(ωt) + j sin(ωt). The real part is cos(ωt), and the imaginary part is sin(ωt): together, they give the coordinates of a point rotating around the unit circle.
Imagine a system that always doubles its input signal. Predict what happens to its output if you send the same input two seconds later.
e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ

That’s Euler’s formula from the review. Returning to the doubling system: sending the input two seconds later makes the doubled output arrive two seconds later too. This property is called time invariance—the system responds the same way regardless of when the input arrives. It’s one of the two properties in LTI, which stands for linear and time-invariant.
I'm not sure. Maybe it means the output only depends on the input?

The key is timing: time invariance means that delaying the input delays the output by the same amount, with its shape unchanged. For the doubling system, an input pulse of height 3 produces an output pulse of height 6 whenever you send it.

Hint: focus on the timing. Imagine sliding the input pulse two seconds to the right on a graph. For a time-invariant system, the output pulse slides two seconds to the right too, keeping its height and shape.
Linear means scaling and adding inputs scales and adds the outputs?

Yes—linearity means scaling and adding inputs produces the same scaling and adding of their outputs. An LTI system has both properties: linearity and time invariance, where delaying the input delays the output by the same amount. Recognizing these systems helps us predict their responses to complicated signals using responses to simpler ones.
Time-invariant means if you delay the input, the output is just delayed by the same amount.
Exactly—the output keeps its shape and shifts by the same amount. Now recall the complete idea from memory.

transcript.text: Because then you can build any input from pieces and add up the responses.
